subject: pe

moments.title: Stoke Mandeville Games
moments.body: Ludwig Guttmann, a Jewish neurologist who had fled Nazi Germany in 1939, runs the Spinal Injuries Centre at Stoke Mandeville Hospital. On 29 July 1948 — the day of the London Olympics opening ceremony — he organises an archery competition for 16 patients (including 2 women), all WWII servicemen and women with spinal injuries.
moments.takeaway: Para-sport was founded by a refugee neurologist as therapy, on the same day as the Olympics he could not compete in.

moments.title: Beijing Paralympics scale up
moments.body: Beijing 2008 marks a step-change in Paralympic broadcasting and participation: 3,951 athletes from 146 countries. The IPC, founded in 1989, has equal IOC partnership. London 2012 sells out almost every Paralympic event for the first time; Channel 4's coverage transforms perception in the UK.
moments.takeaway: Within 60 years, an archery competition for 16 patients became a global mega-event with thousands of elite athletes.

now.title: Para-sport today
now.body: Paris 2024 featured 4,400 Para-athletes from 168 nations. Classification systems (defining functional categories) remain contested and complex. Para-athletes like Tanni Grey-Thompson (UK, 11 Paralympic golds), Ellie Simmonds (UK, swimming), David Weir (UK, wheelchair racing) and Trischa Zorn (US, swimming, 55 medals) have public profiles unimaginable a generation ago.
now.open_questions: How can Para-athletes earn proportionate to Olympic counterparts? Prize money, sponsorship and broadcasting gaps persist.

reflection: Guttmann was 50 when he ran the first games. He won a knighthood (1966) and a posthumous reputation as 'father of the Paralympics'. The man Nazi Germany expelled built one of Britain's most enduring sporting contributions.
